summary: Explores competing uses, architectures, and desirable features of integrated internal trouble ticket systems for network and other operations centers. It is a wishlist of functional requirements, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When something breaks, a help desk writes a ticket. This paper lists what a really good ticket system for network repair crews should be able to do.

subtitle: Building the ideal system for tracking and managing network problems

tldr.problem: Network Operations Centers need to track problems and coordinate fixes among multiple operators on different shifts, but no system fully covers all the features required.
tldr.mechanism: A trouble ticket system acts like a hospital chart for network problems: every update is recorded with timestamps and operator names, tickets can be prioritized, assigned, and escalated, and the data can be mined for statistics about network reliability.
tldr.outcome: This document serves as a wishlist of functional requirements showing what a production-quality NOC tool should be able to do, influencing the design of actual network operations software.

today: RFC 1297 is an Informational RFC documenting requirements and best practices for network operations tools. While published in 1992, its principles remain relevant to NOC design and inform many modern incident management systems.

sections.title: The Problem: Coordinating Network Repairs
sections.content:
A Network Operations Center (NOC) is the central facility where teams of operators monitor networks around the clock and respond to problems. In multi-operator and multi-shift environments, work on a single problem may span hours and involve several different people. Without a structured system, knowledge gets lost: an operator working the night shift fixes part of a problem, but when the day shift arrives, they may not know what was already tried, or they might need to consult with someone who has gone home or is on vacation.

This RFC explores the requirements for an ideal trouble ticket system: a tool that acts like a hospital chart for network problems. It should record a complete history, allow anyone to pick up where someone else left off, track priorities, and eventually produce statistics about network reliability and operational efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network problem happens, multiple people might work on it across different shifts. You need a system like a shared notebook so everyone knows what's been tried and what the next step should be.

sections.title: Core Functions of a Trouble Ticket System
sections.content:
A good trouble ticket system serves multiple purposes. First, it is short-term memory and communication: a centralized record showing the complete history so any operator can come up to speed without calling coworkers. Second, it provides scheduling and work assignment: operators can see all open problems sorted by priority and pick their next task intelligently. Third, it enables referral and dispatching: problems can be assigned to specific engineers or operators by name. Fourth, it acts as an alarm clock: when a ticket is waiting for something (a vendor callback, a site response), a timer can be set to generate an alert if no progress is made.

Beyond these operational benefits, a ticket system provides oversight by specialized personnel, statistical analysis of mean time between failure and mean time to repair for equipment, and accountability for the organization's response to problems. It can also filter alert storms by noting which devices are already known to be down, and it documents the NOC's efforts in case of user complaints.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket system is like a shared logbook that remembers what happened, tells operators what to do next, sends reminders when things are taking too long, and keeps count of how often equipment breaks.

sections.title: Structure of a Ticket and Configuration
sections.content:
A trouble ticket has three main parts. The header contains fixed fields like the time the problem started, the operator who opened it, the severity, and a one-line description. These fields may vary by ticket type: a user complaint ticket looks different from a hardware outage ticket. Headers may also include who reported the problem, which machines and networks are affected, which operator should be assigned, and when to escalate if no progress is made.

The main body consists of incident updates: a series of timestamped free-form text entries by operators describing what they found and what they tried. Early updates might include a complex problem description or pasted diagnostic output; later updates might be simple notes like 'Called site; no answer.' A good system allows the operator to override timestamps if an update is recorded after the fact, and to mark time spent as 'customer time' (waiting for a user) versus 'NOC time' (the team actively debugging), so performance metrics are accurate. Finally, resolution data captures the problem summary, the fix applied, which component failed, and supervisor sign-off.
sections.plainLanguage: A ticket has a header with basic facts, a notes section where operators write what they tried, and a resolution section that explains what was wrong and how it was fixed. Different types of problems can have different ticket formats.

sections.title: Linking Multiple Ticket Types
sections.content:
The NOC might work at multiple levels. A single hardware failure might generate many 'user complaint' tickets from different affected users, all of which point to one 'trouble' ticket tracking the actual hardware problem. Multiple independent hardware problems pointing to a systemic issue (an old router, insufficient redundancy) might be grouped under an 'engineering ticket' documenting the long-term problem. And multiple engineering issues might roll up to a 'meta' ticket about whether the current NOC tools and procedures are adequate. A well-designed system allows all these ticket types to reference each other, showing the full chain from a user's complaint down to the systemic problem and back up.

This hierarchical approach helps both in the moment (operators see related tickets) and in post-mortems (engineers can trace patterns of failures back to their root causes). It also supports different organizations within the larger operations center: many NOCs are responsible for multiple networks, so tickets should link to network, site, and device information.
sections.plainLanguage: Tickets can link to other tickets: one user's complaint might point to the main hardware problem, which points to a bigger engineering issue. This helps teams see patterns and root causes.

sections.title: Integration with Other NOC Tools
sections.content:
For maximum efficiency, the trouble ticket system must integrate with the rest of the NOC environment. Operators need multiple windows open: a ticket, a terminal for debugging, a database query tool, email, and an alert monitor. A ticket should be openable directly from an alert by clicking on a device, with the alert details automatically filled into the header. Conversely, when a ticket times out, its alarm should feed into the alert system so operators get all alerts from one place.

Database connections should populate ticket fields automatically: looking up the network operator's phone number from their login id, finding contact information from a machine name, or getting alarm thresholds from a configuration database. The system should integrate with email so that problem reports arriving by mail can be pasted directly into a ticket, and so scheduled ticket summaries can be emailed to engineers and site representatives. For dispatch, the system should support notifying multiple channels (email, pagers, voice systems) based on the ticket's severity and duration, and should allow direct dispatch of service engineers. Finally, the system should support network access to tickets via email and web-like queries, a subroutine API for custom functionality, and integration with expert systems and graphics tools for reporting.
sections.plainLanguage: A good ticket system works with everything else in the NOC: it opens from alerts, fills in information from databases, sends emails, pages engineers, and gives real-time reports.

sections.title: Operational Requirements and Challenges
sections.content:
The system must be fast: operators need to answer user questions over the phone in real time, so searching for old tickets must take seconds, not minutes. The system must be reliable and always available, with backups running continuously so that a hardware failure does not lose any data. It must scale: old tickets need to be archived after a year or more, but archives should be restorable for historical analysis. Security and privacy are critical: operators must be able to restrict who can see which tickets (some information is sensitive), and the system must log all changes for accountability.

A key operational challenge is the choice between fixed fields and free-form text. Fixed fields make data consistent and searchable, enable automatic verification (ensuring phone numbers have ten digits), and support statistical reports. But too many fixed fields slow operators down and force them into rigid procedures that do not match their actual work. The best approach is to use fixed fields only where they are automatically filled by the system or explicitly used in reports, and to allow ticket types to be customizable by local staff so different NOCs can define formats for their own needs.
sections.plainLanguage: A production system must be fast enough for real-time work, reliable enough to never lose data, secure enough to keep sensitive information private, and flexible enough for different organizations to customize it.
